Definition
In the previous lessons on microprocessors, you learned about basic microprocessor operation and the three basic elements found in microprocessors, the registers, the ALU, and the control section.
INTRODUCTIONM
In this lesson, you will study the 8085 microprocessor in detail. You will learn about the internal structure of the 8085 microprocessor, including the registers, ALU, and control section...
Each of these sections will be described in detail. By understanding each of these sections, your overall understanding of the 8085 will be much greater.

You will also learn about the input/output signals present at each pin of the 8085 IC package. These signals are used to control the external microprocessor system elements and to transfer data between the microprocessor and the rest of the system...

After completing this lesson, you will be able to describe the structure of the 8085 and the features unique to the 8085. For more details on the advanced features of a microprocessor, a manufacturer's data book should be obtained for the 8085...
Let's begin the lesson on 8085 MICROPROCESSOR CIRCUIT.....................
LESSON MENU
8085 MICROPROCESSOR CIRCUITRY
The 8085 is a 8 bit microprocessor. The internal registers are 8 and 16 bits wide. The external data bus 8085 microprocessor is also 8 bits wide.
RESET OUT
DISCUSSION
The 8085 has a 16 bit address bus and thus the 8085 can address up to 2 or 64K bytes of memory.
The functional diagram of the 8085 is shown below..........
HIGHER A8 - A15
LOWER : AD0 - AD7

You can see from the diagram that the sections of the 8085 microprocessor are connected by internal busses. All communications within the microprocessor are performed by the combined effort of the data and control bus...
The address bus is primarily for addressing locations or devices external to the internal system. The data bus of the 8085 is 8 bit wide. This is why the 8085 is known as a 8 bit microprocessor.
Before we examine the sections of the 8085 in detail, let's look at a simple microprocessor instruction. The instruction is:

This instruction adds the 8 bit value in register B to the 8 bit value in the accumulator (register A) and places the result in the accumulator. This one operation causes many things to happen within the microprocessor...
A simplified list of the actions is given below............
a. Put the value of the Program Counter (PC) into the address buffers.
b. Drive Address Latch Enable signal high or low.
c. The /Read signal goes low to indicate a read.
d. Read the 8 bit intruction from the data bus.
a. Move the instruction to the Instruction Register.
c. Generate timing signals for the registers and ALU.
a. Move the 8 bit value of the A register into the ALU.
From this example, you can see that the registers, buffers, control section, ALU, and the internal data bus are all used to add these two numbers.
The operation of these elements must be controlled or coordinated by the control sections of the microprocessor. The microprocessor performs many operations for each instruction that is executed...
In addition to the actions listed, the microprocessor must also check the status of the interrupts and reset while executing the instruction.
Now that you have an idea of what steps the microprocessor must perform for a basic instruction, let's look at the sections of the 8085 microprocessor in detail.
HIGHER A8 - A15
LOWER : AD0 - AD7
It is here that you will see a breakdown of each element in the 8085 block diagram and how they correspond to one another.
REGISTERS

As we saw in the previous example, the registers are where data and addresses are temporarily stored within the microprocessor. The data in the registers can be accessed and changed much faster than data in external memory. Let's look at a brief summary of each register......#
FLAG REGISTER
The accumulator (A register) is used for arithmetic, logic, load and store operations. This is one of the registers used in the previous instruction example.

There are three 16 bit or six 8 bit general purpose registers depending on how you use them. The BC register can be 16 bit, known as BC, or 8 bit as in B or C. B was used in the instruction example provided in this lesson. he registers DE (D & E) and HL (H & L) also work in this manner. When the registers are used in tandem they are called register pairs.
Further, the DE and HL registers also work in this manner. When the registers work in tandem they are called register pairs.
When a 2 or 3 byte instruction is used, you cannot send (for example) the low order 8 bits to the C register and the high order 8 bits the D register. ster.
The full 16 bits must be sent to either the BC register pair or the DE register pair. The same holds true for the HL register pair.its the D register. ster.

There are certain microprocessor instructions that use 16 bit values. Remember, if you write 8 bits into D and you use a 16 bit DE instruction, the contents of E are unknown and will cause incorrect values.ues...

The stack pointer (SP) is a special address register that always points to the top of the stack. A stack is a location in memory where data is stored like a stack of papers. You must take papers off the stack to see what is below them. rther, the BC, DE and HL registers are considered register pairs, and cannot be separated for the same instruction.....

The Program Counter (PC) always points to the memory location of the next instruction to be executed. The register always contains a 16 bit address. at is, when a 2 or 3 byte instruction is used, you cannot send (for example) the low order 8 bits to the C register and the high order 8 bits the D register.

The Flag register contains 8 bits which indicate certain conditions within the system. These conditions are the carry flag (C), the auxiliary flag (AC), the sign flag (S), the zero flag (Z) and the parity flag (P)...
FLAG REGISTER

The carry flag (C) is controlled by the certain arithmetic operations of the microprocessor. If this flag is set (a logic high) it indicates that either a carry (from addition) or borrow (from subtraction) has occurred. The condition of this bit can be tested to determine if an added or subtracted number has borrowed or carried.....

The auxiliary carry flag (AC), also known as the overflow bit, indicates overflow when performing Binary Coded Decimal (BCD) functions. Unlike the carry which indicates overflow in the 8th bit, this indicates overflow from the 4th bit...

In microprocessors, register bits are labeled 0 through 7, or 0 through 15, however big the system allows. This means that the 4th bit (for example) is really bit 3. The graphic below illustrates this..
The sign bit (S), is set according to the 8th bit in the accumulator (A) after an arithmetic or logic operation. The 8th bit can be used to represent the sign of a number.
FLAG REGISTER

The zero flag (Z), is set to 1 when the result of an operation generates zero for a result. In other words, zero in each bit location of the result. This flag is set even if a carry is generated but all bits of the register are zero.

The parity bit (P) is set to 1 if the number of 1 bits in the accumulator (A) is even, and 0 if the number is odd. This makes sure that the information is correct in the system. Parity is a method for error detection...
As you can see, these five flags provide valuable information about the operation of the system after many of the instructions are performed.
Without the flag information, the results of an operation would be known, but any of the conditions or problems with the operation wouldn't.
Without knowing the information regarding that operation, incorrect results could be used by the system, compounding errors in the operations that follow.

Also, not shown, are internal buffers which are used to temporarily hold data or addresses. These buffers hold information the microprocessor needs to process. By storing the information internally processing speed is increased...

Data is transferred between registers or between a registers and another section of the microprocessor on the internal data bus. The control blocks manage the flow of the data within the microprocessor...

ALU The arithmetic/logic unit (ALU) of the 8085 microprocessor performs the arithmetic and logic operations for the system. The ALU can add, subtract, increment, decrement, AND, OR, XOR, comparison, rotation and complement...

Based upon the result of an operation, certain bits will be set or reset within the flag registers. This provides the microprocessor with a way of knowing what occurred during the previous instruction...

After all data has been moved into place the control register allows the ALU to process the data. The result of the operation is placed in a location dictated by the instruction and the control section. The bits of the flag register are set or reset according to the result...
For a complete list of the 8085 arithmetic and logic operations, you should consult an 8085 microprocessor data book.
TIMING AND CONTROL

The timing and control block includes the circuitry to apply the internal clock signals, process the RESET signal, the READY signal and generate the memory control signals. Each of these signals will be covered in greater detail later in this lesson...
RESET OUT
CONTROLNT
In the next lesson you will see how important the signals of this section are to the proper movement of information from external devices to the microprocessor and vice versa.
If the timing is not correct, devices will conflict and incorrect data will result.
INTERRUPT CONTROL
This block allows the microprocessor to stop what it is doing and service an external device such as a keyboard.....
INTERRUPT CONTROLL
Without interrupts, the currently executing program would have to repeatedly check or poll each external device to see if a device was ready to transfer data between itself and the microprocessor.

For example, when you press a key on the keyboard of an IBM personal computer, an interrupt is generated and the computer stops executing the current program and stores the keystroke in a buffer. The computer then continues execution of the program...

The NIDA 8085 microprocessor card set does not use an interrupt for the keyboard. Rather, the keyboard circuits are repeatedly polled to see if a key has been pressed. There are advantages and disadvantages to both methods...
When the microprocessor receives an interrupt, it stops executing the current program and executes another program to specifically deal with that interrupt.
After processing the interrupt the microprocessor returns to the original program.

When an interrupt is called, the interrupt program must do several things so the original program register settings are correct when execution begins again. The list below indicates the minimum number of steps that must be performed by the interrupt program: Save the contents of any general purpose register that will be changed during the interrupt routine. 2. Service the cause of the interrupt. 3. Restore the contents of the registers. 4. Issue a RETURN instruction.....
1. Save the contents of any general purpose register that will be changed during the interrupt routine.
3. Restore the contents of the registers.
4. Issue a RETURN instruction.struction........

These steps provide correct interrupt recovery in the original program. If you modified registers and didn't restore them to their proper values, errors could exist in the main program data once it resumes...
Now that we have looked at the different blocks of the 8085 microprocessor, let's look at the pin configuration (pin out) for the microprocessor..
RESET OUT

The pin configuration of the 8085 is shown below. Note that address pins 12 through 19 are also data pins. Special circuitry will take the correct information from these pins at the proper time during operation. Having two or more signals on one line is known as multiplexing...

Pin 20 is the Ground or reference connection. Pins 12-19 are the A/D0 - A/D7 Multiplexed Address/Data Bus lines. In a machine cycle this bus is the address bus; then it becomes the data bus for the remainder of the cycle...
Pins 21-28 are the A8-A15 signals of the Address Bus. These are the high 8 bits of the address bus. There are no multiplexed data signals on these pins.
Pins 1 and 2 are the XTAL1 and XTAL2 signals which are used to connect an external crystal to the microprocessor. The 8085 has a built in timing circuit which requires an external crystal.
Pin 36 is the RESET IN signal. When this line is set low, the microprocessor resets and the instruction pointer is set to zero.
Pin 3 is the RESET OUT signal. This signal indicates high when the processor is being reset and can be used to reset other devices in the system.
RESET OUT

Pin 4 and 5 are the SOD and SID signals. The SOD or Serial Output Data line is used to send serial data from the microprocessor using the SIM instruction. The SID or Serial Input Data line is used to receive serial data using the RIM instruction...

Pin 7, 8 and 9 are the RST 7.5 RST 6.5 and RST 5.5 External Restart Interrupt connections. A high on these lines indicates a reset to the microprocessor. These interrupts have predefined memory locations where they will execute from. These interrupts can also be turned off using a process called masking...

Pin 6 is the TRAP interrupt. This interrupt cannot be turned off and takes precedence over all other interrupts. This interrupt also has a predefined location where the microprocessor will begin execution of code when the interrupt occurs...

Pin 10 and 11 are the INTR and INTA signals. The INTR is the interrupt request signal. A high on this line indicates a reset is requested from an external device. When the INTA or interrupt acknowledge signal is low, it indicates that the microprocessor acknowledges the request...

Normally, the RST 5.5, 6.5 and 7.5 interrupts are enough for applications requiring the microprocessor. If more are required an interrupt controller is used which connects to the INTR and INTA signal lines. This device must generate the location of where the programs will initiate.

The table below shows the priorities of the interrupt pins. If the microprocessor is servicing an interrupt and then receives a request from one with a higher priority, it will pause its present operation to process the request with the higher priority. After that, the microprocessor will return to its previous operation...

Pin 30 ALE is the Address Latch Enable signal. The address latch IC is a bank of flip-flops used to store the last input value. The address latch stores the address from the multiplexed lines so it will be available for the rest of the cycle. The address latch enable tells the address latch it can take the information from the A/D pins...
RESET OUT
Pin 31, WR, is the Write Control signal. A low level indicates the data on the data bus is to be written to the selected memory address or I/O location.
Pin 32, RD, is the Read Control signal. A low level indicates the selected memory or I/O device is to be read and that the data bus is available for data transfer.

Pin 39 and 38 are the HOLD and HLDA signals. When high, the HOLD signal indicates that another device wants to take control of the address and data bus. This is known as DMA or direct memory access...

The HLDA or Hold Acknowledge signal is used to tell the device that it may take control of the address and data bus as soon the current instruction cycle ends. The microprocessor will not take control again until the HOLD signal is removed...

Pin 37 is the CLK or Clock signal. This signal provides a system clock to other devices in the system. The frequency of this clock is half as much as the crystal frequency. The microprocessor runs at half the speed of the crystal attached to it...

Pin 35 is the READY signal. This signal is used for external memory or devices that are slower than the microprocessor. A low on this line indicates that the device being used is not finished reading or writing and the microprocessor must wait...

When this signal goes high, it indicates to the microprocessor that it may continue with its next operation. is is known as asychnronous communication. In other words, both devices are not synchronized...

Pin 34 is the IO/M signal. When high indicates this pin an IO device is being accessed. When the signal is low, memory is being accessed. This pin is very important for selecting the correct external devices in the system...
Pin 29 and 33 are the S0 and S1 signals. The signals are known as the machine status signals and are used with the IO/M signal in certain situations for proper external circuit operation./
Pin 40 is Vcc for the 8085 microprocessor. This pin delivers +5 volts VDC to the system.

As you learn more about the interface between the microprocessor and external circuitry, the purpose for those signals will be more apparent. In the experiment you will be able to look at any of these signals and compare them with other signals in the system...

0 - F THESE KEYS ARE USED FOR ENTERING HEXADECIMAL NUMBERS. DATA AND ADDRESSES ARE ENTERED USING THESE KEYS.

EDIT THIS KEY IS USED TO EDIT DATA IN RAM. WHEN YOU PRESS THIS KEY, THE LCD WILL SHOW "EDIT ADD:_". THE SYSTEM IS NOW WAITING FOR YOU TO ADD A SEGMENT AND OFFSET. AN EXAMPLE WOULD BE "553:53". THE SEGMENT IS 0553 AND THE OFFSET IS 0053.
RUN THIS KEY IS USED TO EDIT DATA IN RAM. WHEN YOU PRESS THIS KEY, THE LCD WILL SHOW
"RUN ADD: ". THE SYSTEM IS NOW WAITING FOR YOU TO ENTER A SEGMENT : OFFSET TO
TO THE PROGRAM.
ENTER THIS KEY IS USED TO INDICATE A CURRENT PROGRAM, THAT YOU HAVE FINISHED ENTERING INFORMATION FOR A PARTICULAR TASK.
STOP THIS KEY IS USED WHEN YOU FINISH ENTERING DATA INTO RAM OR WANT TO EXIT A PROGRAM. AFTER PRESSING STOP, THE DISPLAY WILL RETURN TO THE "NIDA CORPORATION INTEL 8086 VX.X" MESSAGE.

Remember, when the RESET signal is applied to the 8085 microprocessor, it instructs the internal instruction register to go back to the beginning. This then has a jump command that leads the instruction pointer to the Nida monitor program...
In this portion of the experiment, you will use the microprocessor to add two numbers as an illustration of the 8085's arithmetic capabilities.
13. Press RESET on the PC130-485 Card. You will be entering a program into memory for execution by the 8085 microprocessor.

Entering programs into memory of the 8085 uses the EDIT function of the monitor Program. Once you have pressed EDIT, you will be asked to enter an address to edit. Typically, the address will be 1000...

On the screen is the current address that you are looking at and the current value stored in that location. There are three things you can do at any address. Enter a new value and press enter, press the down arrow to move to the next address or use the up arrow to move to the previous address...
Every time you enter a value and press enter, you will automatically move to the next address. If you just press enter without entering data, this will put zeros for that memory location.I

Always remember to use the up and down arrows for movements through your code. When a program is shown to you, you will be given an address, opcodes, mnemonics and a description. Start at the first address given and enter each opcode consecutively until you are finished...
A mnemonic is what an assembler program uses to generate the opcodes for a program. Once you are finished editing your program you can press STOP.
14. Enter the following program into memory starting at "1000" (EDIT, 1000, enter values with an ENTER after each one, pressd STOP when finished).
1000 3E MVI A, #0Ah Moves the value 0Ah into the A register.
1002 06 MVI B, #05h Moves the value 05h into the B register.
1005 4F MVI C, A Moves value in A into C.
1006 C9 RET Return to the monitor program.

Remember, the values of 0Ah and 05h were placed into the A and B registers. Then the microprocessor added them together and stored the result in the accumulator and also copied it to the C register. This replaced the value previously stored there...

The program you are using shows you the values in the A, F (Flag), B and C registers. The value in B is 0Ah and the value in C is the result 0Fh. The accumulator changed because the result of all arithmetic operations is placed there...
You can go back and change the values stored at 1001 and 1003. These are the memory locations of the data to be added. By changing these, you can observe different additions in the system....
